Last Updated: 2024–2026

---

Definition of cancer
- Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably, invade nearby tissues, and can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymph system. - Normally, cells follow genetic instructions that tell them when to grow, divide, and die. When DNA changes or mutations happen, those instructions can become faulty, and the cell may begin dividing too much instead of stopping when it should. - The spread of cancer cells to other organs is called metastasis, which is one of the main causes of cancer-related deaths. How cancer develops
- Cancer develops through a multi-stage process that begins with changes in a cell's DNA. These genetic mutations may occur because of:
- - Errors during cell division
- - Exposure to harmful substances such as tobacco smoke or radiation
- - Inherited genetic mutations from parents
- - Viral or bacterial infections
- - Environmental and lifestyle factors
- As abnormal cells continue to divide, they can form tumors and eventually spread through the bloodstream or lymphatic system to other parts of the body. Common types of cancer
- There are more than 100 types of cancer. Some of the most common types include:
- 1. Carcinoma - Cancer that begins in epithelial cells, such as lung cancer, breast cancer, and colorectal cancer. - 2. Sarcoma - Cancer that develops in bones, muscles, fat, or connective tissues. - 3. Leukemia - Cancer of the blood-forming tissues, especially the bone marrow and blood cells. - 4. Lymphoma - Cancer that affects the lymphatic system and immune cells. - 5.

Leukemia - Cancer of the blood-forming tissues, especially the bone marrow and blood cells. - 4. Lymphoma - Cancer that affects the lymphatic system and immune cells. - 5. Melanoma - A type of skin cancer that develops in pigment-producing cells called melanocytes. - Common cancers are the cancers diagnosed most often in a population. A widely used list includes breast, prostate, lung, colon and rectal, melanoma, bladder, kidney, endometrial, leukemia, pancreatic, thyroid, liver, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer statistics
- In 2022, there were about 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide. By 2050, new cases are projected to rise to about 35 million if population growth continues. - Lung cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 2022, with about 2.5 million new cases, followed by breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach cancers. Lung cancer was also the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. - Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), nearly 10 million people died from cancer in 2022. - Most common cancers in 2022: Lung cancer, Breast cancer, Colorectal cancer, Prostate cancer, Skin cancer (non-melanoma), Stomach cancer. - Leading causes of cancer death: Lung cancer, Colorectal cancer, Liver cancer, Breast cancer, Stomach cancer. - Approximately 400,000 children develop cancer each year worldwide. Main risk factors
- Cancer risk factors are things that increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not mean a person will definitely get cancer. - - Age. Risk rises as people get older. - - Tobacco use. Smoking and other tobacco products strongly increase cancer risk. - - Alcohol use.

- Cancer risk factors are things that increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not mean a person will definitely get cancer. - - Age. Risk rises as people get older. - - Tobacco use. Smoking and other tobacco products strongly increase cancer risk. - - Alcohol use. Regular heavy drinking raises the risk of several cancers. - - Family history and inherited genes. Some cancers run in families because of inherited gene changes. - - Obesity and inactivity. Excess body weight and low physical activity increase the risk of several cancers. - - UV exposure. Sunlight and tanning beds increase skin cancer risk. - - Infections. HPV and some other infections can increase cancer risk. - - Environmental exposures. Radon, asbestos, secondhand smoke, and certain chemicals can raise risk. Prevention strategies
- Cancer prevention strategies focus on lowering exposure to known risk factors and catching some cancers early, when treatment works best. - - Do not use tobacco. Avoid smoking and secondhand smoke. - - Maintain a healthy weight. Excess body weight raises the risk of several cancers. - - Be physically active. Regular movement and less sitting help reduce risk. - - Eat a healthy diet. Emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and beans; limit fast foods, red meat, processed meat, and sugary drinks. - - Limit alcohol. Less alcohol means lower cancer risk. - - Protect yourself from the sun. Use shade, clothing, and sunscreen to reduce skin cancer risk. - - Get vaccinated. HPV and hepatitis B vaccines can prevent cancers linked to these infections. - - Use screening tests. Tests like mammograms, Pap tests, colonoscopy, and low-dose CT can find some cancers early.

---

TNM staging system
- The TNM staging system is a standard way to describe how far a cancer has spread. It was developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) and the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC). - What TNM means
- - T (Tumor) = size and extent of the primary tumor. - - N (Nodes) = whether nearby lymph nodes contain cancer. - - M (Metastasis) = whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. - Details of TNM Classification
- - Primary Tumor (T)
- - - TX: Primary tumor cannot be assessed
- - - T0: No evidence of a primary tumor
- - - Tis: Carcinoma in situ (early-stage cancer limited to the original cell layer)
- - - T1–T4: Increasing size or local spread of the tumor
- - Regional Lymph Nodes (N)
- - - NX: Nearby lymph nodes cannot be assessed
- - - N0: No cancer found in nearby lymph nodes
- - - N1–N3: Increasing spread to nearby lymph nodes
- - Distant Metastasis (M)
- - - M0: No distant metastasis detected
- - - M1: Cancer has spread to distant organs or tissues
- How it is written
- - TNM is usually written with numbers and letters, such as T2N1M0. In that example, the tumor is moderately sized, there is some lymph node involvement, and there is no distant metastasis.

- - A cancer classified as T2N1M0 means: The tumor is moderately sized, Cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, No distant metastasis has been found
- Why it matters
- - Doctors use TNM to help estimate prognosis, choose treatment, and communicate clearly about cancer stage. It is especially used for solid tumors, while some cancers like blood cancers or brain tumors may use different staging systems. Stage 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 definitions
- Stage 0
- - Stage 0 is also called Carcinoma in situ (CIS). Abnormal cells are present, but they have not spread into nearby tissue. It is often called carcinoma in situ, and it may become cancer later if untreated. This stage is highly treatable and often curable. - Stage 1
- - Stage 1 usually means the cancer is small and confined to the original site. It has not spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant organs. There is little or no spread to nearby lymph nodes. - Stage 2
- - Stage 2 means the tumor is larger than stage 1 and may have started to spread into nearby tissue or a small number of nearby lymph nodes, depending on the cancer type. - Stage 3
- - Stage 3 means the cancer is more advanced locally. It has often grown deeper into nearby tissues and may involve more nearby lymph nodes, but it has not yet spread to distant organs.

a small number of nearby lymph nodes, depending on the cancer type. - Stage 3 - - Stage 3 means the cancer is more advanced locally. It has often grown deeper into nearby tissues and may involve more nearby lymph nodes, but it has not yet spread to distant organs. The cancer has spread extensively to nearby tissues and/or multiple lymph nodes, but not to distant parts of the body. - Stage 4
- - Stage 4 means the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. This is also called metastatic cancer. Stage IV is known as metastatic cancer. The cancer has spread to distant organs such as the lungs, liver, bones, or brain. How staging affects treatment
- Early stage
- - Stage 0 and stage I cancers are often treated with local treatments such as surgery, radiation, or both, because the cancer is still limited to one area. - Middle stages
- - Stage II and stage III cancers often need a combination of treatments, such as surgery plus chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy, because there is a higher risk of spread or recurrence. - Advanced stage
- - Stage IV cancers have spread to distant organs, so treatment is usually mainly systemic therapy, such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, sometimes with radiation or surgery for symptom control. - Why staging matters
- - Staging also helps doctors estimate prognosis, plan follow-up, and decide whether the goal is cure, long-term control, or symptom relief. Grading vs staging
- Staging tells you how much cancer is in the body and where it has spread. Grading tells you how abnormal the cancer cells look under the microscope and gives an idea of how fast they may grow.

- - Staging is about the extent of cancer: tumor size, nearby lymph nodes, and distant spread. It is often described with the TNM system or with stage numbers 0 to 4. - Grading
- - Grading is about the appearance of the cancer cells. Lower-grade cancers look more like normal cells, while higher-grade cancers look more abnormal and are often more aggressive. - Importance of accurate staging
- Accurate staging is important because it helps doctors choose the right treatment, estimate prognosis, and decide whether surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination is most appropriate. - Why accuracy matters
- - If a cancer is under-staged, treatment may be too weak and miss disease that has already spread. If it is over-staged, a patient may get more intensive treatment than needed, which can increase side effects without improving benefit. - Treatment planning
- - Staging tells the team whether the cancer is still localized or has reached lymph nodes or distant organs. That changes the treatment goal from mainly local control to broader systemic therapy when needed. - Prognosis and trials
- - Accurate staging also helps doctors estimate likely outcomes and identify clinical trials that match the true extent of disease. It is also important for comparing results across patients and treatment centers.

General cancer warning signs
- General cancer warning signs include unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, a new lump or thickening, unusual bleeding or discharge, a sore that does not heal, changes in bowel or bladder habits, persistent cough or hoarseness, and ongoing pain without a clear cause. - Common warning signs
- - Unexplained weight loss or weight change. - - Fatigue that does not improve with rest. - - New lump or swelling anywhere in the body. - - Unusual bleeding or discharge. - - A sore that does not heal. - - Changes in bowel or bladder habits. - - Persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing. - - Skin changes, including a changing mole or a new skin lesion. - Important note
- - These symptoms do not always mean cancer, because many non-cancer conditions can cause the same problems. The key concern is when a symptom is new, lasts a long time, or keeps getting worse.

- Early detection matters because cancer found sooner is usually smaller, less spread out, and easier to treat successfully. - Why it helps
- - Treatment is often more effective when the cancer is still at an early stage. - - Early treatment can offer more options, including local treatment like surgery in some cases. - - It can reduce treatment intensity, side effects, and long-term complications. - - It can improve survival and quality of life. - Screening vs symptoms
- - Early detection can happen through screening before symptoms appear, or by noticing warning signs and getting checked early. This is important because some cancers do not cause obvious symptoms until they are more advanced. - Simple example
- - A breast cancer found at stage 1 is often much easier to treat than one found after it has spread, which is why early screening and prompt evaluation of new symptoms can make a major difference. When to seek medical attention
- Symptoms worth checking
- - A new lump or swelling. - - Unexplained weight loss. - - Persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing. - - Unusual bleeding or discharge. - - A sore that does not heal. - - Changes in bowel or bladder habits. - - Ongoing pain without a clear cause. - - Fever, night sweats, or major fatigue that does not improve.

Symptom variations by stage
- Early stages
- - Stage 0 to stage I cancers may cause no symptoms at all, or only subtle local signs such as a small lump, a skin change, abnormal bleeding, or a mild change in bowel or bladder habits. Because the disease is still limited, symptoms are often easier to miss or confuse with non-cancer problems. - Middle stages
- - Stage II and stage III cancers are more likely to cause symptoms from the growing tumor or nearby spread, such as pain, swelling, coughing, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or enlarged lymph nodes. At these stages, symptoms tend to be more noticeable because the cancer is affecting surrounding tissue or regional nodes.

Last Updated: 2026

---

Surgery
- Cancer surgery can be used to remove the whole tumor, remove part of a tumor to reduce symptoms or help other treatments work better, or take tissue for diagnosis and staging. It is a local treatment, so it works best for solid tumors in one area rather than cancers that have spread widely. - Common roles
- - Curative surgery: aims to remove all visible cancer. - - Debulking surgery: removes as much cancer as possible when full removal is too risky or not possible. - - Palliative surgery: helps relieve pain, pressure, bleeding, or blockage. - - Diagnostic/staging surgery: helps confirm cancer and see how far it has spread. - How it fits with other treatment
- - Surgery is often combined with chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy. These treatments may be given before surgery to shrink the tumor, or after surgery to destroy any remaining cancer cells. - When it may not be used alone
- - Surgery is usually not enough by itself for cancers that have already spread to distant organs, and it is generally not used to treat leukemia in the same way as solid tumors. Chemotherapy
- Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing and dividing. - How it works
- - Chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, which is why it can shrink tumors and slow cancer spread. It may damage the cell’s DNA or interfere with cell division so the cancer cell cannot keep multiplying.

It may damage the cell’s DNA or interfere with cell division so the cancer cell cannot keep multiplying. - How it is used
- - It can be given before surgery to shrink a tumor, after surgery to destroy remaining cancer cells, together with radiation or surgery, or to control cancer that has spread. - Common side effects
- - Because chemotherapy also affects some healthy fast-growing cells, common side effects include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, mouth sores, hair loss, low blood counts, infection risk, constipation or diarrhea, and nerve tingling. - Simple example
- - If a tumor is too large for surgery at first, chemotherapy may be used first to make it smaller, then surgery may follow. Radiation therapy
- Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy radiation, usually X-rays, to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. - How it works
- - Radiation damages the DNA of cancer cells, so they can no longer divide normally and eventually die. It does not kill cells instantly; the damage builds up over days or weeks of treatment. - How it is used
- - It may be used as the main treatment, before surgery to shrink a tumor, after surgery to kill leftover cancer cells, together with chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms such as pain or trouble breathing. - Main types
- - External beam radiation therapy: radiation is delivered from a machine outside the body. - - Internal radiation therapy (brachytherapy): radioactive material is placed inside or near the tumor.

- - Side effects depend on the treatment area, but can include skin irritation, tiredness, appetite loss, nausea, and local tissue inflammation. - Simple example
- - If a tumor is in one area and surgery is difficult, radiation may be used to target that spot precisely and reduce the tumor size. Immunotherapy
- Immunotherapy is a cancer treatment that helps the body’s immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. - How it works
- - Cancer cells can hide from immune defenses or switch off immune responses. Immunotherapy helps by boosting immune activity, removing the “brakes” on immune cells, or giving the immune system specially designed agents to attack cancer more effectively. - Main types
- - Checkpoint inhibitors: block proteins that stop immune cells from attacking cancer. - - CAR-T or T-cell therapy: modifies immune cells so they can better target cancer. - - Monoclonal antibodies: lab-made antibodies that mark cancer cells or block growth signals. - - Cancer vaccines and other immune boosters: help the immune system respond more strongly. - When it is used
- - Immunotherapy is often used for cancers that have spread, come back, or do not respond well to other treatments. It can also be combined with surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation in some cases. - Side effects
- - Because it stimulates the immune system, side effects can include fatigue, skin changes, flu-like symptoms, or inflammation in organs such as the lungs, liver, intestines, or thyroid.

- Targeted therapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to attack specific molecules, genes, or proteins that help cancer cells grow and spread. - How it works
- - Unlike chemotherapy, which can affect many fast-growing cells, targeted therapy is designed to hit a more specific cancer feature, so it often causes less damage to normal cells. It may block growth signals, stop tumor cells from dividing, or cut off signals that help the tumor form new blood vessels. - When it is used
- - Targeted therapy is often used when the cancer has a known biomarker or mutation that the drug can attack. It can be used alone or combined with surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy depending on the cancer type and stage. - Common types
- - Monoclonal antibodies: bind to targets on the outside of cancer cells. - - Small-molecule drugs: enter the cell and block internal signaling pathways.

- Combination treatments use two or more cancer therapies together, such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, to improve the chance of controlling or curing the cancer. - Why combinations are used
- - Different treatments attack cancer in different ways, so combining them can improve effectiveness, reduce resistance, and treat both local and spread disease. For example, surgery or radiation can remove or destroy cancer in one area, while drugs can treat cancer cells that may have spread elsewhere. - Common patterns
- - Neoadjuvant therapy: treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumor. - - Adjuvant therapy: treatment given after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells. - - Concurrent therapy: treatments given at the same time, such as chemotherapy with radiation. - Examples
- - A common combination is surgery plus chemotherapy, or radiation plus chemotherapy for certain cancers. Some cancers may also use targeted therapy with immunotherapy or chemotherapy when studies show better outcomes.

Some cancers may also use targeted therapy with immunotherapy or chemotherapy when studies show better outcomes. - Main tradeoff
- - Combination treatment can be more effective, but it may also cause more side effects, so doctors choose the mix based on cancer type, stage, biomarkers, and the patient’s overall health. - Simple idea
- - Combination therapy is like using multiple tools at once: one treatment may shrink the tumor, another may kill leftover cells, and another may reduce the chance of the cancer returning. Clinical trials
- Clinical trials are research studies in people that test new ways to prevent, detect, diagnose, or treat cancer. - Why they matter
- - Clinical trials help determine whether a new treatment is safe and effective, and they are a major way cancer care improves over time. They can also test new combinations of existing treatments and better ways to manage side effects. - Main types
- - Treatment trials: test new drugs, procedures, or treatment combinations. - - Prevention trials: look for ways to reduce cancer risk. - - Screening/diagnostic trials: improve early detection and diagnosis. - - Supportive care trials: improve comfort, side effect control, and quality of life. - Trial phases
- - Phase 1: focuses on safety and dose in a small group. - - Phase 2: looks at whether it works and continues safety monitoring. - - Phase 3: compares the new treatment with standard care in a larger group.

- - Clinical trials are not only for people with no other options; many studies test new combinations or earlier use of treatments that may benefit people at different stages. - Simple idea
- - A clinical trial is a carefully monitored study that helps answer, “Does this new cancer approach work better, work safer, or improve quality of life?”.
